content.text:
# The Symbiosis of Theory and Practice: AI's Dual Role in Modern Mathematics

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into the scientific landscape has sparked a profound debate regarding the nature of human creativity, the definition of "research," and the future of intellectual discovery. Two recently published articles on arXiv, "Mathematics in the age of AI" by Terence Tao and "Disproof of the Yau--Tian--Donaldson conjecture" by Jihao Liu, offer a fascinating and complementary study of this transition. While one serves as a philosophical meditation on the meta-context of mathematics, the other stands as a concrete, groundbreaking realization of AI-augmented discovery. Together, they represent the two sides of a new era: the reflection and the realization.

Terence Tao’s essay, delivered at the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians, takes a high-level, philosophical approach. Rather than engaging in the typical "human vs. machine" debate over whether AI *can* do math, Tao adopts a pragmatic stance: he conditions on the reality that research-level AI tools will arrive. His primary inquiry is orthogonal to capability; he asks what the goals and values of mathematical research actually are. By using the problem-solving component of mathematics as a case study, Tao challenges the community to reconsider the "why" of mathematics. If a machine can solve a problem, does the human's role shift from "solver" to "architect," "curator," or "explorer"? Tao’s work is a vital piece of intellectual infrastructure, providing the ethical and philosophical framework necessary for mathematicians to navigate a world where the "grunt work" of proof-finding may be automated.

In stark contrast, Jihao Liu’s "Disproof of the Yau--Tian--Donaldson conjecture" provides the practical evidence for the very capabilities Tao contemplates. This is not a meta-commentary but a technical tour de force in differential geometry. Liu constructs a polarized smooth projective fivefold to disprove a major conjecture regarding constant scalar curvature Kähler metrics. The significance of this work is doubled by its methodology: Liu explicitly acknowledges that the main result was obtained using generative AI, specifically citing GPT-5.6-sol, Fable 5, and the Danus system. This paper is a landmark because it moves AI from a "tool of convenience" to a "partner in breakthrough." It demonstrates that AI can navigate the immense complexity of high-dimensional geometry to produce results that were previously thought to be within the exclusive domain of human intuition.

The relationship between these two papers is symbiotic. Tao provides the "soul" of the new era—the questions of value, purpose, and the preservation of mathematical meaning—while Liu provides the "body"—the tangible, hard-won results that redefine the boundaries of the possible. Tao warns us to think about what we value when the difficulty of the "how" is diminished; Liu shows us exactly what happens when that "how" is revolutionized. 

Ultimately, these two works suggest that the future of mathematics will not be a replacement of the human mind, but a radical expansion of its reach. We are entering a period where the mathematician's primary skill may shift from the manual execution of complex derivations to the high-level synthesis of ideas and the curation of AI-generated insights. By reading these papers together, we see a complete picture: the birth of a new mathematical paradigm where philosophy and technology are no longer at odds, but are instead the dual engines of progress.
